topic: Trans-Saharan Ostrich Expedition, South African feather crash

slides.title: In 1911, a government sent a secret mission for the perfect feather.

slides.body:
By 1913, ostrich feathers were its fourth most valuable export, after gold, diamonds and wool.

But the finest plumes came from elsewhere: the Barbary ostrich, a wild bird from around the Sahara.

slides.kicker: So parliament paid for a mission.
slides.body:
Russell Thornton, a Boer War veteran, could spend up to £7,000 on 150 birds. Rumour said the Americans were after them too.

The condition: if he got caught, the government would deny everything.
At Zinder, after six weeks of talks, the French said no. No live birds. No eggs.

Exactly how is still unclear. Local contacts seem to have helped, and Thornton's family denies any smuggling.

The birds were marched hundreds of miles, then shipped south. About 140 survived.

slides.kicker: Two years later, the market was gone.
slides.body:
Open-top cars made giant hats impractical. War brought austerity. Fashion moved on.

By 1914, the plumes were practically worthless. Thousands lost their jobs.

Thornton's flock was never bred into South Africa's herds.

The country's ostriches fell from over 775,000 in 1913 to about 32,000 by 1930. The last of Thornton's birds was killed by lightning.

slides.lead: We prepare for the rivals we can see.
slides.accent: The bigger risk is that people stop wanting what we sell.

slides.line: Save this for the next time you're perfecting the wrong thing.

caption:
In 1911, South Africa's parliament funded a secret expedition to bring back Barbary ostriches, the source of the finest feathers in the world. The birds made it home. Then cars, war and fashion killed the feather trade.

What's something you worked hard to perfect, just as it stopped mattering?
